Nadroga beats Ra to claim Farebrother Sullivan Trophy
item.description: An electric atmosphere filled Narauyaba Ground in Rakiraki as approximately 12,000 spectators gathered to witness Nadroga successfully claim the Inkk Farebrother Sullivan Trophy with a hard-fought 28-20 victory over Ra. Nadroga got off to a strong start, scoring the opening try in the third minute through their blindside flanker to take an early 5-0 lead.
item.content:encoded:
An electric atmosphere filled Narauyaba Ground in Rakiraki as approximately 12,000 spectators gathered to witness Nadroga successfully claim the Inkk Farebrother Sullivan Trophy with a hard-fought 28-20 victory over Ra.

Nadroga got off to a strong start, scoring the opening try in the third minute through their blindside flanker to take an early 5-0 lead.

However, Nadroga were shown a yellow card in the 10th minute after deliberately knocking the ball out of the hands of Ra scrum-half Peni Matawalu.

Ra dominated possession during the first 30 minutes and turned that pressure into points in the 17th minute when their outside centre crossed the try line to level the scores at 5-5.

Nadroga continued to surrender possession through ill-discipline and were shown a second yellow card, this time to their prop.

Despite the setbacks, Nadroga regained the lead with three minutes remaining in the first half, scoring their second try through a powerful driving maul from a lineout to extend their advantage to 10-5.

Nadroga started the second half strongly, scoring their third try in the 44th minute through their blindside winger.

Ra were awarded a penalty in the 49th minute, which their fullback successfully converted to reduce the deficit to 15-8.

Nadroga responded with another try in the 55th minute through their loose forward, extending their lead to 20-8 .

They continued to dominate the scoreboard, scoring their fourth try in the 68th minute to stretch their advantage to 25-8 .

Ra refused to give up, responding with a try through their winger before their prop crossed the try line for another, narrowing the deficit to 20-25 and putting pressure on the defending champions.

However, a late penalty awarded to Nadroga gave them the opportunity to seal the victory.

They opted to kick for goal, successfully extending their lead to secure a 28-20 win.

item.title: Bill will die with current Parliament if rejected - Rabuka
item.description: The Constitution Amendment Bill will move to a referendum if it receives two thirds of Parliament’s support but will die with the current Parliament if rejected. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has made this clear as he acknowledges concerns that some members of the public may not have been heard during earlier consultations.
item.content:encoded:
The Constitution Amendment Bill will move to a referendum if it receives two thirds of Parliament’s support but will die with the current Parliament if rejected.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has made this clear as he acknowledges concerns that some members of the public may not have been heard during earlier consultations.

Rabuka made the comments during the Special Parliamentary Committee sitting at Tuva Primary School, where members of the public were given another opportunity to share their views on the proposed changes to Fiji’s Constitution.

He says the outcome of the parliamentary vote will determine the next step in the process, with approval allowing the Bill to proceed to a referendum.

However, if MPs vote against it, the Bill will remain there and die with the current Parliament.

He says Fiji’s desire to continue reviewing its Constitution will remain, and Members of Parliament are free to raise their concerns and propose amendments if they have enough support in the House.

Rabuka also points out that the Constitution provides for periodic reviews, allowing the country to revisit its constitutional arrangements in the future.

He says a review has already been carried out, with Attorney-General Sevuloni Valenitabua serving as the commissioner of the review commission.

Rabuka says the commission’s report was taken to Cabinet before being brought to Parliament, and the proposed Bill has gone through considerable scrutiny.

He says the committee has returned to conduct further consultations because there are concerns that some people may still feel their views were not heard during the earlier process.

Rabuka says the committee will first listen to the public’s submissions before proceeding with its usual committee processes and procedures.

Meanwhile, Mata ni Tikina of Malomalo, Emoni Rokomoce, says he has participated in the consultation process and has been informing the tikina about the proposed constitutional changes.

Rokomoce says they agree with the changes and the consultation process, adding that they are grateful that the Great Council of Chiefs is recognised as lawful.

He also says the people need the Constitution to be changed.

item.title: Farmers given one week to apply for six El Niño assistance initiatives
item.description: Farmers are encouraged to practise mulching, minimum tillage, water harvesting, effective irrigation and maintaining soil cover to reduce moisture loss and protect their crops as the Ministry of Agriculture rolls out six initiatives to support those affected by El Niño. Farmers also have one week to apply for assistance under the Ministry of Agriculture, Waterways and Sugar Industry's El Niño Resp
item.content:encoded:
Farmers are encouraged to practise mulching, minimum tillage, water harvesting, effective irrigation and maintaining soil cover to reduce moisture loss and protect their crops as the Ministry of Agriculture rolls out six initiatives to support those affected by El Niño.

Farmers also have one week to apply for assistance under the Ministry of Agriculture, Waterways and Sugar Industry's El Niño Response Initiatives.

Minister for Agriculture Tomasi Tunabuna says the initiatives are designed to protect farmers' livelihoods, sustain agricultural production, strengthen household food security and support farming families most vulnerable to prolonged dry weather.

The six initiatives cover emergency farm water and irrigation, livestock feed, water and animal health, climate-resilient planting materials and seeds, climate-smart agriculture and soil moisture, household and community food security, and sugar sector drought protection.

Under the emergency farm water and irrigation initiative, assistance will include water tanks, emergency water delivery, water conveyance systems, irrigation kits and sugarcane irrigation where technically appropriate.

For livestock farmers, the Ministry will provide support through livestock feeding systems, silage, supplementary feed, livestock water, strategic de-stocking advice, bee feed and essential animal treatment.

The climate-resilient planting materials initiative will support access to suitable planting materials for dalo, yams, vegetables, kumala, rice and cassava, while strategic multiplication blocks will be established to improve future availability.

Under climate-smart agriculture and soil moisture, farmers will be encouraged to adopt practical measures such as mulching, minimum tillage, cover crops, protective cropping, drip irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties and water harvesting.

The household and community food security initiative will support home gardening, backyard farming, community nurseries and communal food production, particularly for households facing pressure on their food supplies.

The sugar sector drought protection initiative will focus on trash retention, minimum tillage, crop stress mapping, crop checks, targeted irrigation, wildfire advisories and access to suitable early-maturing seed cane.

Tunabuna says the initiatives were developed after the Ministry received reports from agriculture stations, extension offices, industry representatives and farmers' organisations about declining water availability, crop losses, deteriorating pastures, livestock feed shortages, pressure on household food supplies and reduced farm incomes.

He says the Ministry assessed where the impacts were most severe, which farming households were most vulnerable and what assistance was urgently required before reallocating its budget, personnel and activities.

Farmers who are genuinely affected are encouraged to review the three prospectuses covering the six initiatives and apply for assistance that best addresses their immediate farming or household needs.

The expression of interest period will initially remain open for one week, after which the Ministry will assess the number, locations and nature of applications received to determine whether the application period should be extended.

Tunabuna stresses t ha t submitting an expression of interest does not automatically guarantee assistance, as applications will be assessed based on eligibility, field verification, technical suitability, severity of the impact and the availability of resources.

He is also asking farmers to provide complete and accurate information to ensure assistance is distributed fairly and transparently, while minimising bias, potential conflicts of interest and duplication.

Meanwhile, the Ministry has convened the Fiji Food Security Cluster, bringing together stakeholders to share information, coordinate efforts and identify ways to assist farmers, exporters, households and consumers affected by El Niño .

Tunabuna says the effects of El Niño go beyond individual farms and can also affect food availability, market supplies, food prices, exports and household incomes.

He says the Ministry is also working with the World Food Forum Fiji Youth Chapter, the Fiji Women Farmers Network, civil society organisations and community representatives to ensure the response includes women farmers, young people, people living with disabilities, minority groups, remote communities and vulnerable households.

Tunabuna says the six initiatives are the first stage of the Ministry's targeted response, with further assistance or adjustments to be considered depending on monitoring, applications received and available resources.

He is also urging farmers and communities to use water responsibly, protect water sources, follow wildfire advisories and avoid unnecessary burning.

item.title: Vaturu Dam levels drop as drought expected to continue into January - Ro Filipe
item.description: Water levels at Vaturu Dam in Nadi have continued to drop, with the drought situation in the Western Division expected to persist into December and possibly January. Minister for Public Works Ro Filipe Tuisawau says the dam is one of the key critical infrastructure supplying water to the Nadi and Lautoka areas, and its declining levels are being closely monitored.
item.content:encoded:
Water levels at Vaturu Dam in Nadi have continued to drop, with the drought situation in the Western Division expected to persist into December and possibly January.

Minister for Public Works Ro Filipe Tuisawau says the dam is one of the key critical infrastructure supplying water to the Nadi and Lautoka areas, and its declining levels are being closely monitored.

Following three days of assessment of the drought situation in the West, Ro Filipe is urging members of the public to conserve water and prepare for worsening conditions in the coming months.

He says the weather forecast indicates that the situation is unlikely to improve, with other water sources also drying up.

Ro Filipe says the Water Authority of Fiji continues to deliver water to affected communities, while the National Disaster Risk Management Office is coordinating the whole-of-government response.

He says the Government is also organising assistance packages as part of its response to the situation.

Ro Filipe is urging not only households but also businesses and hotels to take precautionary measures, conserve water and store it safely .

He says the situation remains critical and people need to be prepared as the drought continues to affect water sources across the country.

Meanwhile, overnight water rationing will begin in parts of Nadi and Lautoka from 9pm tonight as prolonged dry weather and declining water levels continue to put pressure on water supply in the Western Division.

The Water Authority of Fiji says rationing will take place daily from 9pm to 4am until further notice to allow reservoirs to recover overnight and ensure water is available during the day.

In Lautoka, affected areas include Natabua, Natokowaqa, Field 40, Rifle Range, Saru, Vuda, Wairabetia, Waiyavi, the Lautoka Central Business District, Tavakubu, Buabua, Teidamu and surrounding areas.

In Nadi, affected areas include Sabeto, Namaka, Martintar, Saunaka, Nawaka, Nadi Town, Denarau, Narewa, Wailoaloa and parts of southern Nadi extending to Momi .

The Authority is urging residents and businesses to conserve water immediately by avoiding non-essential activities such as washing vehicles, watering lawns and filling swimming pools.

item.title: FWCC hits back at Ro Filipe Tuisawau
item.description: Temalesi Vono , Rashika Kumar · 14/11/2026 Civil society organisations do not need seats in Parliament to influence policy, question government decisions and scrutinise legislation.
item.content:encoded:
Temalesi Vono , Rashika Kumar · 14/11/2026

Civil society organisations do not need seats in Parliament to influence policy, question government decisions and scrutinise legislation.

This has been highlighted by the Fiji Women’s Crisis Centre (FWCC) criticising Minister for Public Works, Ro Filipe Tuisawau’s comments accusing NGOs of crossing the line.

The FWCC says civil society groups have an important role in shaping laws and policies and representing the concerns of ordinary people.

FWCC Coordinator Shamima Ali says they take offence at Ro Filipe's remarks.

Ali says rights-based civil society organisations and NGOs serve as a bridge between ordinary people and the policies that govern them.

She says their role is not to seek political power but to ensure those in authority are questioned and their decisions are scrutinised.

Ali adds that politics is not limited to membership of political parties, but also involves bringing about positive changes for society and the people.

She says civil society groups have every right to question the Government, noting that their members also vote in elections and pay taxes that contribute towards the salaries of parliamentarians.

Ali has also reminded Ro Filipe that Fiji is a democratic country, not a dictatorship, and says freedom of speech and expression gives people the constitutional right to speak out.

FWCC says Ro Filipe was elected by the people, including members of civil society, and has a responsibility to serve them.

Ro Filipe has told the civil society organisations to read the clarifications on centralised voting during the general elections from legitimately elected representatives in Parliament rather than from unelected commentators or civil society whose actions and misleading statements undermine the democracy they purport to uphold.

He says some NGO leaders are confused and they need to make a decision now on whether to remain a NGO leader or become a politician and stand in elections.

The Centre for Democracy and Dialogue, Fiji Council of Social Services, Fiji Women’s Rights Movement, Social Empowerment and Education Programme, FemLINKpacific and Transparency and Integrity Fiji have strongly condemned the Government’s amendment to the Electoral Act 2014 last Friday permitting ballot papers to be counted at centralised counting centres rather than at the polling stations where votes are cast.

The organisations say they consider this one of the most concerning and regressive amendments to Fiji’s electoral framework, introducing unnecessary risks of electoral manipulation and undermining the transparent and independently verifiable vote-counting procedures established over the last three general elections.

They say the amendment introduces a new section 89A, allowing the Electoral Commission to approve the counting of ballot papers at one or more counting centres instead of polling stations, and to approve special procedures for such counting.

They say in simple terms, ballot boxes containing uncounted votes can now be moved away from polling stations, transported to another location, stored and eventually opened and counted elsewhere.

The organisations say this fundamentally changes the safeguards that have protected the integrity of Fiji’s election-day voting process.
